story_text.value:
Hello HN!

My name is Sam and this is Craig. Craig is a local-first TUI for managing AI coding agents. It’s agent-agnostic, creates isolated worktrees by default, and has a rich CLI for the agent to interact with to manipulate state and perform actions in the TUI.

I started building Craig when I got a job offer at a shop that was using Cursor. I was previously using Claude Code with Conductor and really enjoyed this type of experience. However Conductor didn’t support Cursor at the time and I wasn’t a big fan of the Cursor 3 Agents interface. For personal projects I was using mostly Codex with some Claude Code. Switching between tooling was frustrating. Around the same time I also started really enjoying the agent CLIs and how they just “felt good”.

Craig kind of builds on that and I think of it as a heads-up display and controls around the CLI. With the TUI being keyboard-driven you can get into a nice multi-task flow and move around pretty quickly. The UX is made to be low friction and high signal-to-noise.

To get started you can run `npm install -g craig-cli`, launch your favorite terminal (I like Ghostty), pop it in fullscreen and run the `craig` command. Once you launch it you can create a workspace, this can be a single repo directory or multiple. Then create a new task under the workspace to launch Cursor, Codex, or Claude. Do your thang, and use your agent to create a PR. You’ll see Craig automatically sync that PR, poll for checks and let you know when the PR is ready to merge. Merge it and keep moving in the same thread or start a new one.

I’d love for you to give it a try and let me know what you think - any feedback is greatly appreciated.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I kept watching the Tesla Roadster's flying video and wondered how much force would be required to pull off a stunt like that since it seemed unreal to me, so I asked Claude Opus 5.5 to create a simulation for me.

I gave Opus one task: look at the video and create a simulation like that using three.js, matching the video as closely as possible. I'd thought that Opus would one- or two-shotted this since in my mind it was just estimating height and distances and working backwards to compute the thrusts. Little did I know this would turn into a multi-day project.

Opus's first hurdle was recognizing the five parked Tesla vehicles. The video was dark, so it was hard for Opus to see. I helped it identify the models and also gave it the approximate dimensions of all six Tesla vehicles, including the Roadster.

1. The initial version looked close enough to the video, but Opus made the car fly straight, whereas the video shows the Roadster veering to the left and landing to its left, so I asked Opus to watch the video again and correct that.

2. The next version showed the car drifting to the left mid-flight like the video, but the position was off when I compared frame by frame to the video. It turned out that Opus was being lazy and used only a few frames as reference instead of doing it frame by frame.

3. Once Opus matched the car position to the video, frame by frame, I realized that the roll did not match, so I asked Opus to investigate and redo.

4. The next version had the position and roll correct, but I did not see any thrusters firing during flight. It turned out that Opus was creating a smooth trajectory where the thrusters only fired for the launch and the landing, and stayed off mid-flight. This was not what I'd seen in the video, however.

5. Opus then changed it so that the thrusters would fire during the flight, which would affect the trajectory continuously. However, at this point I realized something odd: it was firing a thruster upward, which is in the opposite direction of the four bottom-mounted thrusters. It was definitely strange since the video did not show any upward-firing thrusters. It turned out that Opus was using 12 thrusters in total because it relied on Elon Musk's comment in 2018 that the Roadster would have around 10 thrusters. Using 12 thrusters was what allowed it to create any trajectory it wanted to. I asked it to use only 6 thrusters: four bottom ones for lifting and landing, and two side thrusters mounted near the front wheels since those were the ones I could see firing in the video.

6. Opus gave me another simulation with 6 thrusters firing, but now I could not see the side thrusters firing at all during the flight, which is similar to #4. It turned out that up to this point, Opus had been doing the simulation under the ideal conditions where the trajectory was pre-computed instead of doing a closed-loop control and constantly adjusting the thrust to keep the car on the planned path. Opus then added wind gusts and redid the simulation using a 100 Hz feedback loop.

At this point, I have something that is close enough to the video. It is still not perfect since I would love to match the firing sequence, intensity, and cloud shape of the thrusters during the flight, but I think this is a good stopping point for me, and now I have something where I can tweak the params like the car's weight, max thruster force, max height, number of rolls, etc. and model any flight path I'd like. There are a lot of params to configure, and some combinations can result in invalid flight paths, so I added WebMCP so that we can use the Claude plugin for Chrome to drive the simulation and ask the AI any questions. I found that Sonnet 5.5 Medium is good enough for this. Haiku 5.5 Medium is fast but also makes mistakes.

Caveats: the mass, drag coefficients, thruster positions and gas performance are estimates, not Tesla data. The closed-loop model also assumes perfect sensors.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

In Keen Code, a coding agent solo-developed by me, I have implemented a task-classifier using Jev and a simple auto-router based on the classification result. The article shares details about how it's implemented.

In short, it has a very simple idea:

- For every user message, ask Jev to classify the task in one of the three categories (simple, standard, complex) given current state of the conversation.

- Keen also asks Jev to put a probability on this question: "is this a new task?"

- Based on the result, Keen uses a heuristic to switch the current model to one of the three pre-configured models by user for the three categories

- To make the router work, users have to configure one model per task category inside the coding agent itself

The heuristic is also very simple:

When routing is enabled, Keen switches only if the selected-category probability is greater than 0.5 and either:

- new-task probability is at least 0.6; or - category probability is greater than 0.8 and the target category is a higher tier than the active routed model.

Thoughts and feedback are welcome. And if you are interested to know more about Keen Code, the repo can be found here: https://github.com/mochow13/keen-code

story_text.value:
I never felt comfortable signing up for cloud budgeting apps and having them store all of my financial data on their servers. I also didn't find locally hosted options that I liked using.

That led me to build Maali (https://maali.app) over the past year. It is currently a Mac and Windows app that lets you track spending, budgets, recurring bills, income, net worth, and more. It stores all of your data on your computer.

You can bring your data in by either manually importing bank statement files (CSV/PDF), or by using SimpleFIN, a third-party bridge that you set up once and it keeps your data in sync. Since SimpleFIN introduces a third party that moves your data, I also added a power-user feature where Maali watches a folder (per account) and imports files dropped there, so you can automate downloads however you like and keep everything local.

It also has an optional AI analyst (local Gemma 4 E4B model) that provides commentary on your spending and flags anything unusual about your finances.

I realize that mobile is a big part of convenience for people. Maali lets you set up a phone web app over your own Tailscale network, paired by QR code. I'm also close to launching iOS/Android mobile apps that keep data in sync between the desktop/mobile apps using end-to-end encryption. My goal is to provide a great user experience with maximum convenience without sacrificing privacy.

The full app is free to use for 30 days (no card/signup needed). After that, if you find it useful and want to continue using it, it's $99 one-time. There's a live demo on the site (https://maali.app/today) with synthetic data so you can get a feel for it. Would love to hear any feedback that you have.

story_text.value:
Dovepass answers one question for drone operators: given two points, can a drone legally fly between the two points?

I build route planning for delivery drivers and wanted to check what it would look like if the vehicle flies. Drone navigation is different from land-based vehicle navigation. In addition to road and traffic data, it requires data on buildings, building height, wind speed and direction, and total load, including the payload a drone might carry. It is also governed by a set of rules; depending on the area, federal, state, or county rules may apply.

The decision point becomes whether, at each point on the route the drone can fly based upon whether regulations permit, the wind direction favours it and whether it flying over a road or people? Depending on when the drone flies, the same path valid two hours ago may no longer be valid.

For example a trip from 24th & Valencia ( Mission) to 19th Ave & Irving (Inner Sunset) and back is 5.1 km each way. A DJI mini 4 Pro would take 19 min on 7 mph winds from the west and use 92% of its usable battery and give a Go signal with warning. But at 11mph wind from the same direction would become No-Go because it would use 111% of its usable battery. Or whenever there is a Giants game at Oracle Park, this route is unusable because it is 2.5miles from the stadium. FAA bars all drones within 3 nautical miles from a stadium from 1 hour before the game to one hour after it ends.

I chose San Francisco as the first city to build this because there is enough data about the buildings (92% coverage), wind data is easily available at the drone flying height, and the city has a mix of slopes, water bodies, buildings and airport-related airspace restrictions all in one city. The city also has local rules regarding drone flights in parks - both operated by the city as well as by Golden Gate National recreational areas ( National Park Service).

I used kimi to build it and claude acted a sa judge. To understand more about the challenges faced during the build and the tradeoffs made please read - https://dovepass.com/how-it-was-built/"

The city also has local rules regarding drone flights in parks - both operated by the city as well as by Golden Gate National recreational areas ( National Park Service).

I used kimi to build it and claude acted a sa judge. To understand more about the challenges faced during the build and the tradeoffs made please read - https://dovepass.com/how-it-was-built/"
